title: The brothers' songs
hookLine: poems of the first monks: forests, rain, freedom

lines: THE SISTERS' BOOK HAS A COMPANION.
cards: Rain on a thatched roof. A peacock calling somewhere in the trees. A man sitting alone in a forest, saying out loud that he is free.

These aren't scenes from a novel. They're lines from poems that Buddhist tradition gives to the early monks themselves. The sisters' songs, the Therigatha, have a companion: a book of the brothers' songs.
Today it opens, and today's word is its name.

teach.h: THERA, AN ELDER. GATHA, A VERSE.
teach.b: First, the name. Theragatha. A thera is an elder, a senior monk, and a gatha is a verse: verses of the elders.

teach.h: EACH POEM CARRIES A MONK'S NAME.
teach.b: Each poem carries a monk's name, and tradition says the monk himself spoke it, often about the moment he was freed, or looking back on the road there. So these aren't sermons about the monks.
They're his own words, in the first person: I went to the forest, I sat, I was set free. Third, what they sing about.
Forests. Caves and rocky hills. Clouds and rain.
Peacocks, elephants, cranes. And again and again, freedom: the work is done, the burden is down, there is nothing more to do. Some poems are a single verse.
Some run on for pages, and in one of them a monk argues with his own mind. Fourth, how to read them. Some readers find them strangely close: a man in a hut, listening to the rain, and glad.
Others notice how much they repeat, the same phrases closing poem after poem, almost like a chorus.

teach.h: A CHORUS, AND ONE MAN'S AFTERNOON.
teach.b: Both are there: a shared chorus, and one person's afternoon of rain and peacocks. The brothers' book sits beside the sisters' among the short texts of the Pali canon.
In the days ahead come some of these brothers by name: a monk with a dry roof, a man who swept away old flowers, a former bandit, an actor, the great disciples.
Each one, in his own words.

how: In Theravada communities, verses from the Theragatha are read and taught alongside the Therigatha, and teachers often draw on single poems from it as short reflections.

practice: Read one short poem slowly, once, out loud if you can: something from an old book or a new one, or a poem you've known by heart since school.

Then put it down, sit, and let one line stay with you, not its meaning, just its sound or its picture: rain, a hill, a bird. When the mind wanders off, come back to that line the way you'd come back to the breath.
